claim: Lymnaea stagnalis has been used extensively since the 1970s to study the functioning of the nervous system from molecular signalling to behaviour.
source: One particularly well-suited mollusc for this type of research is the freshwater pond snail, Lymnaea stagnalis, which has been used extensively since the 1970s to study the functioning of the nervous system from molecular signalling to behaviour.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about the historical use of this organism in neuroscience research.

claim: L. stagnalis has been recognized in fields including host-parasite interactions, ecotoxicology, evolution, developmental biology, genome editing, 'omics' and human disease modelling.
source: The value of L. stagnalis also has been recognised in a wide range of applied biological fields. These include the study of host–parasite interactions, ecotoxicology, evolution, developmental biology, genome editing, 'omics' and human disease modelling.
evidence: The claim is supported by knowledge of the diverse applications of this model organism across multiple research fields.

claim: L. stagnalis was initially described by Linnaeus in 1758 as Helix stagnalis.
source: Initially described by Linnaeus in 1758 as Helix stagnalis, the species now known as L. stagnalis is generally referred to as the great pond snail (Panpulmonata; Hygrophila; Lymnaeidae).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to historical taxonomic literature and established knowledge.

claim: L. stagnalis is found throughout Northern America, Europe, and parts of Asia and Australia.
source: It is found throughout Northern America, Europe, and parts of Asia and Australia (Atli and Grosell, 2016; Zhang et al., 2018a; Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and visual evidence in Figure 1 showing geographic distribution.

claim: L. stagnalis inhabits stagnant and slowly running shallow waters rich in vegetation.
source: The snails inhabit stagnant and slowly running shallow waters rich in vegetation and are mainly herbivores, preferring algae, water plants and detritus (Lance et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on habitat preferences.

claim: L. stagnalis are mainly herbivores, preferring algae, water plants and detritus.
source: The snails inhabit stagnant and slowly running shallow waters rich in vegetation and are mainly herbivores, preferring algae, water plants and detritus (Lance et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on feeding behavior.

claim: L. stagnalis are active all year round, even when there is a layer of ice on the water.
source: They are active all year round (even when there is a layer of ice on the water) but typically reproduce from spring to late autumn (Nakadera et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on seasonal activity patterns.

claim: L. stagnalis typically reproduce from spring to late autumn.
source: They are active all year round (even when there is a layer of ice on the water) but typically reproduce from spring to late autumn (Nakadera et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on reproductive seasonality.

claim: L. stagnalis do not have a clear day-night rhythm but display sleep-like behaviour.
source: They do not have a clear day-night rhythm, but display sleep-like behaviour (Stephenson and Lewis, 2011) and are more likely to lay eggs during daytime (Ter Maat et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on circadian patterns and sleep behavior.

claim: L. stagnalis are more likely to lay eggs during daytime.
source: They do not have a clear day-night rhythm, but display sleep-like behaviour (Stephenson and Lewis, 2011) and are more likely to lay eggs during daytime (Ter Maat et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on egg-laying behavior.

claim: L. stagnalis are light to dark brown in colour.
source: They are light to dark brown in colour and relatively large for pond snail species, with their spiral shells reaching lengths of up to 55 mm (Benjamin, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published descriptive literature.

claim: L. stagnalis spiral shells can reach lengths of up to 55 mm.
source: They are light to dark brown in colour and relatively large for pond snail species, with their spiral shells reaching lengths of up to 55 mm (Benjamin, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published morphological data.

claim: In highly oxygenated water, L. stagnalis absorb oxygen directly across their body wall.
source: In highly oxygenated water, they absorb oxygen directly across their body wall; but when dissolved oxygen levels drop, they switch to breathing via a lung accessed by a respiratory orifice called the pneumostome (Lukowiak et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on respiratory physiology.

claim: When dissolved oxygen levels drop, L. stagnalis switch to breathing via a lung accessed by a respiratory orifice called the pneumostome.
source: In highly oxygenated water, they absorb oxygen directly across their body wall; but when dissolved oxygen levels drop, they switch to breathing via a lung accessed by a respiratory orifice called the pneumostome (Lukowiak et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on respiratory physiology.

claim: L. stagnalis serves as the intermediate host for parasites including flatworms responsible for fascioliasis and cercarial dermatitis in humans.
source: L. stagnalis serves as the intermediate host for parasites including flatworms responsible for diseases such as fascioliasis (liver fluke and river rot) and cercarial dermatitis (swimmer's itch) in humans (Adema et al., 1994; Davison and Blaxter, 2005; Ferté et al., 2005; Núñez et al., 1994; Skála et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on host-parasite relationships.

claim: Penetration of a parasite into L. stagnalis initiates a chronic infection in which the parasite alters snail neurophysiology, metabolism, immunity, growth and reproduction.
source: Laboratory and field studies showed that penetration of a parasite into a snail will initiate a chronic infection in which the parasite alters snail neurophysiology, metabolism, immunity, growth and reproduction (Kryukova et al., 2014; Langeloh and Seppälä, 2018; Vorontsova et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published laboratory and field studies.

claim: Primary predators of L. stagnalis juveniles and adults include leeches, crayfish and fish.
source: Primary predators of juveniles and adults include leeches, crayfish and fish, some of which snails can detect via chemicals that the predators emit (Dalesman and Lukowiak, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on predator-prey interactions.

claim: L. stagnalis can detect some predators via chemicals that the predators emit.
source: Primary predators of juveniles and adults include leeches, crayfish and fish, some of which snails can detect via chemicals that the predators emit (Dalesman and Lukowiak, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on chemical detection.

claim: L. stagnalis embryos develop inside transparent eggs packaged in a translucent gelatinous mass.
source: Embryos develop inside transparent eggs packaged in a translucent gelatinous mass allowing observers to follow their developmental stages in detail over the 11–12 days to hatching.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about embryonic development.

claim: L. stagnalis embryonic development from laid eggs to hatching takes 11-12 days.
source: Embryos develop inside transparent eggs packaged in a translucent gelatinous mass allowing observers to follow their developmental stages in detail over the 11–12 days to hatching.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about developmental timing.

claim: The time from laid eggs to mature reproductive adults in L. stagnalis can be as short as two months depending on temperature, photoperiod, feeding regime and mate availability.
source: The time from laid eggs to mature reproductive adults can be as short as two months depending on the temperature, photoperiod, feeding regime and mate availability at the location where they are being raised.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about developmental rates and environmental influences.

claim: In their natural habitat, L. stagnalis have been found to reach an age in excess of one year.
source: In their natural habitat, they have been found to reach an age in excess of one year, but in the laboratory they live longer, up to two years (Janse et al., 1988; Nakadera et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on lifespan in natural populations.

claim: In the laboratory, L. stagnalis live up to two years.
source: In their natural habitat, they have been found to reach an age in excess of one year, but in the laboratory they live longer, up to two years (Janse et al., 1988; Nakadera et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on laboratory lifespan.

claim: The largest and longest-maintained L. stagnalis breeding facility is found at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam, where the species has been bred continuously for over 50 years.
source: The largest and longest-maintained breeding facility is found at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam, where L. stagnalis has been bred continuously for over 50 years (Nakadera et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published information about breeding facilities.

claim: L. stagnalis embryonic development consists of six main stages: cleavage, blastula, gastrula, trochophore, veliger and metamorphosis.
source: (A) The embryonic development in the egg from zygote to hatching (over 11–12 days) is depicted in the white area of the life cycle and consists of six main stages: cleavage, blastula, gastrula, trochophore, veliger and metamorphosis (Source data from Ivashkin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation and visual representation in Figure 2A.

claim: L. stagnalis is a simultaneous hermaphrodite with male reproductive organs functional before the female ones.
source: Although L. stagnalis is a simultaneous hermaphrodite, the male reproductive organs are functional before the female ones (Koene and Ter Maat, 2004): specimens reach male and female maturation on average at an age of 30 and 60 days, respectively (based on Koene, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on reproductive development.

claim: L. stagnalis specimens reach male maturation on average at an age of 30 days.
source: Although L. stagnalis is a simultaneous hermaphrodite, the male reproductive organs are functional before the female ones (Koene and Ter Maat, 2004): specimens reach male and female maturation on average at an age of 30 and 60 days, respectively (based on Koene, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on sexual maturation timing.

claim: L. stagnalis specimens reach female maturation on average at an age of 60 days.
source: Although L. stagnalis is a simultaneous hermaphrodite, the male reproductive organs are functional before the female ones (Koene and Ter Maat, 2004): specimens reach male and female maturation on average at an age of 30 and 60 days, respectively (based on Koene, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on sexual maturation timing.

claim: In the wild, most L. stagnalis individuals are born during the spring and summer seasons and generations partly overlap.
source: An integrated laboratory and field study showed that, in the wild, most individuals are born during the spring and summer seasons and generations partly overlap because the latter cohorts overwinter and overlap with mature individuals of the new spring cohort (Figure 2B; Nakadera et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an integrated laboratory and field study and visual representation in Figure 2B.

claim: L. stagnalis has helped understand mechanisms underlying shell formation.
source: This snail has helped us to understand the mechanisms underlying shell formation (Hohagen and Jackson, 2013), the transfer of non-genetic information to the developing embryos (Ivashkin et al., 2015), and resource allocation during development (Koene and Ter Maat, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on shell formation.

claim: L. stagnalis has helped understand the transfer of non-genetic information to developing embryos.
source: This snail has helped us to understand the mechanisms underlying shell formation (Hohagen and Jackson, 2013), the transfer of non-genetic information to the developing embryos (Ivashkin et al., 2015), and resource allocation during development (Koene and Ter Maat, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on epigenetic information transfer.

claim: L. stagnalis has helped understand resource allocation during development.
source: This snail has helped us to understand the mechanisms underlying shell formation (Hohagen and Jackson, 2013), the transfer of non-genetic information to the developing embryos (Ivashkin et al., 2015), and resource allocation during development (Koene and Ter Maat, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on developmental resource allocation.

claim: L. stagnalis is a simultaneous hermaphrodite, meaning mature individuals express a functional male and female reproductive system at the same time within one body.
source: This snail is a simultaneous hermaphrodite, meaning that mature individuals express a functional male and female reproductive system at the same time within one body.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about the reproductive biology of the species.

claim: Despite having two functional sexes, L. stagnalis specimens copulate unilaterally with one individual playing the male role and the other the female role within one mating interaction.
source: Despite having two functional sexes, specimens copulate unilaterally; one individual plays the male role and the other the female role within one mating interaction (Hoffer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on mating behavior.

claim: There is no obligate alternation of sexual roles in L. stagnalis, but when both individuals of a mating pair are motivated to mate in the male role they can perform a second copulation with the same partner in the opposite sexual role.
source: There is no obligate alternation of sexual roles, but when both individuals of a mating pair are motivated to mate in the male role they can perform a second copulation with the same partner in the opposite sexual role (Koene, 2010; Ter Maat et al., 2012; Van Duivenboden and Maat, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on mating behavior and sexual role flexibility.

claim: Both age and size significantly affect the sex role decision in L. stagnalis under laboratory conditions.
source: The same study showed that both age and size significantly affected the sex role decision under laboratory conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a study showing statistical significance of age and size effects.

claim: L. stagnalis is quite fecund in the laboratory, with snails from the mass culture in Amsterdam producing a large number of offspring all year round.
source: This species is quite fecund in the laboratory: snails from the mass culture in Amsterdam produce a large number of offspring all year round (Nakadera et al., 2014); however, an initial field study found a more moderate fecundity rate in natural populations (Nakadera et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on laboratory fecundity.

claim: An initial field study found a more moderate fecundity rate in natural L. stagnalis populations compared to laboratory populations.
source: This species is quite fecund in the laboratory: snails from the mass culture in Amsterdam produce a large number of offspring all year round (Nakadera et al., 2014); however, an initial field study found a more moderate fecundity rate in natural populations (Nakadera et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published field research on fecundity.

claim: In the laboratory, L. stagnalis specimens produce on average 2-3 egg masses per week each containing 100-150 eggs, depending on the body size of the individual.
source: In the laboratory, specimens produce on average 2–3 egg masses per week each containing 100–150 eggs, depending on the body size of the individual (Nakadera et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on reproductive output.

claim: The hatching rate of L. stagnalis under laboratory conditions is generally above 90%.
source: The hatching rate under laboratory conditions is generally above 90% (Hoffer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on hatching success.

claim: Based on laboratory, semi-field and field studies, explicit inbreeding or self-fertilisation depression for L. stagnalis have been found to be absent or very unlikely.
source: Based on laboratory, semi-field and field studies, explicit inbreeding or self-fertilisation depression for this species have been found to be absent (Coutellec and Lagadic, 2006; Escobar et al., 2011; Koene et al., 2008; Puurtinen et al., 2007) or very unlikely (Coutellec and Caquet, 2011), however the reasons for this remain unclear (Box 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies across different experimental settings.

claim: L. stagnalis eggs are preferentially outcrossed with sperm from mating partners, which can be stored for two months.
source: Nevertheless, eggs are preferentially outcrossed with sperm from mating partners, which can be stored for two months, and individuals only use their own 'autosperm' when this 'allosperm' is not available (Nakadera et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on sperm usage patterns.

claim: L. stagnalis individuals only use their own 'autosperm' when 'allosperm' from mating partners is not available.
source: Nevertheless, eggs are preferentially outcrossed with sperm from mating partners, which can be stored for two months, and individuals only use their own 'autosperm' when this 'allosperm' is not available (Nakadera et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on sperm usage patterns.

claim: L. stagnalis was described as 'a reductionistic, yet sophisticated model to address fundamental questions in learning and memory'.
source: L. stagnalis emerged shortly afterwards, and was described as "a reductionistic, yet sophisticated model to address fundamental questions in learning and memory" (Rivi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published characterization of the model system.

claim: The central nervous system of L. stagnalis is organised in a ring of 11 interconnected ganglia with approximately 25,000 neurons.
source: The relatively simple central nervous system of L. stagnalis is organised in a ring of 11 interconnected ganglia (Figure 3A,B) with ~25,000 neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about neuroanatomy and visual representation in Figure 3.

claim: L. stagnalis neurons are mostly large (30-150 µm in diameter) and their bright, orange-coloured cell bodies are located on the surface of the ganglia.
source: The neurons are mostly large (30–150 µm in diameter) and their bright, orange-coloured cell bodies are located on the surface of the ganglia (Figure 3B; Kemenes and Benjamin, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research and visual evidence in Figure 3B.

claim: Individual neurons and their synaptic connectivity were identified as parts of circuits controlling behaviours in L. stagnalis.
source: Individual neurons (Figure 3C; Benjamin and Crossley, 2020) and their synaptic connectivity were identified as parts of circuits controlling behaviours (Audesirk et al., 1985; Benjamin, 2012; McCrohan and Benjamin, 1980a; McCrohan and Benjamin, 1980b; Syed and Winlow, 1991; Syed et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research and visual representation in Figure 3C.

claim: The molecular pathways involved in memory formation in L. stagnalis were recently identified.
source: The molecular pathways involved in memory formation in L. stagnalis were recently identified, providing further evidence the mechanisms of learning and memory consolidation are conserved across phylogenetic groups in a variety of learning paradigms, including non-associative or associative learning, and operant or classical conditioning (Benjamin and Kemenes, 2013; Fulton et al., 2005; Josselyn and Nguyen, 2005; Kemenes and Benjamin, 2009; Kemenes et al., 2002; Marra et al., 2013; Michel et al., 2008; Nikitin et al., 2008; Park et al., 1998; Pirger et al., 2010; Pirger et al., 2014a; Pirger et al., 2014b; Ribeiro et al., 2003; Rivi et al., 2020; Sadamoto et al., 1998; Sadamoto et al., 2010; Schacher et al., 1988; Vigil and Giese, 2018; Wan et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by extensive citations to published research on molecular mechanisms of memory.

claim: The mechanisms of learning and memory consolidation are conserved across phylogenetic groups in a variety of learning paradigms.
source: The molecular pathways involved in memory formation in L. stagnalis were recently identified, providing further evidence the mechanisms of learning and memory consolidation are conserved across phylogenetic groups in a variety of learning paradigms, including non-associative or associative learning, and operant or classical conditioning (Benjamin and Kemenes, 2013; Fulton et al., 2005; Josselyn and Nguyen, 2005; Kemenes and Benjamin, 2009; Kemenes et al., 2002; Marra et al., 2013; Michel et al., 2008; Nikitin et al., 2008; Park et al., 1998; Pirger et al., 2010; Pirger et al., 2014a; Pirger et al., 2014b; Ribeiro et al., 2003; Rivi et al., 2020; Sadamoto et al., 1998; Sadamoto et al., 2010; Schacher et al., 1988; Vigil and Giese, 2018; Wan et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by extensive citations to published research providing evidence of conservation across species.

claim: Recent studies have revealed differences in learning ability at the behavioural level between laboratory and field situations in L. stagnalis.
source: Recently studies have also revealed differences in learning ability at the behavioural level between situations in the laboratory and the field (e.g., Dalesman and Lukowiak, 2012; Dalesman et al., 2015; Dalesman, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research comparing laboratory and field learning.

claim: L. stagnalis behaviours are generated by reflexive and central pattern generator networks similar to those of vertebrates.
source: Also, since their behaviours are generated by reflexive and central pattern generator networks similar to those of vertebrates (Katz and Hooper, 2007), results from snails offer insights into the fundamental processes important for these animals too.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on neural network organization and inference about similarity to vertebrates.

claim: Recent developments have enabled L. stagnalis to be used as a model for understanding the basis of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Finally, recent developments have enabled this species to be used as a model for understanding the basis of neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: The claim is supported by knowledge of recent research applications.

claim: Comparative analyses have yielded several homologs to human genes linked to ageing and neurodegenerative diseases in Aplysia californica.
source: Comparative analyses have yielded several homologs to human genes linked to ageing and neurodegenerative diseases in A. californica and this species has proved well suited for studying these processes (Moroz et al., 2006; Moroz and Kohn, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published comparative genomic research.

claim: Similar molecular sequences to human genes linked to ageing and neurodegenerative diseases have been identified in L. stagnalis.
source: Similar molecular sequences have been identified in L. stagnalis (Fodor et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on molecular sequences.

claim: L. stagnalis is highly suitable for studying the biological mechanisms of ageing, age-related memory loss and neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases.
source: With the appropriate genetic background, its accessible central nervous system and relatively long and well-characterised life span mean L. stagnalis is highly suitable for studying the biological mechanisms of ageing, age-related memory loss and neurodegenerative diseases, such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases (Arundell et al., 2006; de Weerd et al., 2017; Ford et al., 2017; Hermann et al., 2007; Hermann et al., 2020; Maasz et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2006; Pirger et al., 2014b; Scutt et al., 2015; Vehovszky et al., 2007; Yeoman and Faragher, 2001; Yeoman et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on ageing and neurodegenerative disease models.

claim: Molluscs are the second most diverse animal group and considered to be excellent indicators of ecosystem health.
source: Molluscs the second most diverse animal group and considered to be excellent indicators of ecosystem health.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about mollusc diversity and their use as bioindicators.

claim: L. stagnalis is a sensitive and reliable species for ecosystem health studies.
source: For example, L. stagnalis is a sensitive and reliable species for such studies (Amorim et al., 2019), in a large part because of its well-characterised developmental and reproductive biology as described above.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on ecotoxicological applications.

claim: L. stagnalis has been recognized as a useful organism to examine the effects of pharmacologically active compounds and micro- and nanoplastics on aquatic organisms.
source: L. stagnalis has also been recognised as a useful organism to examine the effects of pharmacologically active compounds and micro- and nanoplastics on aquatic organisms (Amorim et al., 2019; Charles et al., 2016; Ducrot et al., 2014; Gust et al., 2013a; Horton et al., 2020; Pirger et al., 2018; Zrinyi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on toxicological applications.

claim: Molluscs do not have functional oestrogen receptors.
source: However, it must be pointed out that researchers need to be critical of the generalisability of results while performing such experiments since there are differences between the endocrine system of molluscs and vertebrates; molluscs, for example, do not have functional oestrogen receptors (Eick and Thornton, 2011; Lagadic et al., 2007; Scott, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on mollusc endocrinology.

claim: L. stagnalis is the first aquatic non-arthropod invertebrate model organism to be recognised in environmental risk assessments.
source: Notably, L. stagnalis is the first aquatic non-arthropod invertebrate model organism to be recognised in environmental risk assessments.
evidence: The claim is supported by knowledge of regulatory recognition.

claim: The developed standard reproduction test for L. stagnalis was officially approved by the national coordinators of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.
source: The developed standard reproduction test was officially approved by the national coordinators of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD, 2016) thus paving the way for investigating ecotoxicological effects in more detail.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to official OECD approval.

claim: Left-right asymmetry is a general evolutionary phenomenon seen across a variety of species, including humans where the congenital condition situs inversus results in the mirrored position and shape of the heart and liver.
source: Left-right asymmetry is a general evolutionary phenomenon seen across a variety of species, including humans where the congenital condition situs inversus results in the mirrored position and shape of the heart and liver (Blum et al., 2014; Oliverio et al., 2010; Palmer, 2009; Palmer, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on asymmetry across species.

claim: The coil or chirality of snail shells is one of the more spectacular outward manifestations of left-right asymmetry.
source: The coil or chirality of snail shells is one of the more spectacular outward manifestations of this asymmetry.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about shell chirality as a manifestation of asymmetry.

claim: Snails found in nature can have shells that coil either to the right or left, with most species being right-coiling.
source: Snails found in nature can have shells that coil either to the right or left, with most species being right-coiling.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about shell coiling patterns.

claim: Left-winding L. stagnalis specimens are rare and often categorised as 'unlucky' because their different chirality makes it difficult for them to mate with the more usual, right-winding individuals.
source: Specimens of L. stagnalis that coil in the opposite left-winding, or sinistral, direction are rare and often categorised as 'unlucky' because their different chirality makes it difficult for them to mate the more usual, right-winding individuals (Davison et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on mating difficulties related to chirality.

claim: Left-winding L. stagnalis snails are less able to learn in a mate-choice context.
source: Left-winding snails are also less able to learn in a mate-choice context (Koene and Cosijn, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on learning differences related to chirality.

claim: Genes and signalling pathways that are responsible for snail coiling have been identified in L. stagnalis.
source: The existence of the two different morphs has made this species ideal for studying chiromorphogenesis, i.e. the first step of left-right symmetry breaking. Genes and signalling pathways that are responsible for snail coiling have been identified (Abe et al., 2014; Davison et al., 2016; Kuroda, 2014; Kuroda, 2015; Kuroda et al., 2016), and similar signalling pathways are required for vertebrate chiromorphogenesis as well (Kuroda, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on the genetics of chirality.

claim: Similar signalling pathways to those responsible for snail coiling are required for vertebrate chiromorphogenesis.
source: Genes and signalling pathways that are responsible for snail coiling have been identified (Abe et al., 2014; Davison et al., 2016; Kuroda, 2014; Kuroda, 2015; Kuroda et al., 2016), and similar signalling pathways are required for vertebrate chiromorphogenesis as well (Kuroda, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on conservation of chiromorphogenesis pathways.

claim: Selection of sexual traits that affect mating success was previously considered not to act in simultaneous hermaphrodites.
source: Selection of sexual traits that affect mating success was previously considered not to act in simultaneous hermaphrodites (Charnov, 1979; Darwin, 1871; Greeff and Michiels, 1999; Morgan, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to historical literature on sexual selection theory.

claim: Recent research, including work with L. stagnalis, has contradicted the earlier conclusion that sexual selection does not act in simultaneous hermaphrodites.
source: However, recent research, including work with L. stagnalis, has contradicted this earlier conclusion (Anthes et al., 2010; Baur, 1998; Chase, 2007; Janicke et al., 2016; Michiels, 1998; Nakadera and Koene, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent published research contradicting earlier theory.

claim: Experiments with L. stagnalis showed that the mating system seems largely male-driven.
source: Experiments with L. stagnalis showed that this mating system seems largely male-driven, and that the sexual selection gradients are consistently positive for the male function but change over time to benefit the opposite sex (Anthes et al., 2010; Hoffer et al., 2017; Janicke et al., 2016; Pélissié et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published experimental research on mating systems.

claim: Sexual selection gradients in L. stagnalis are consistently positive for the male function but change over time to benefit the opposite sex.
source: Experiments with L. stagnalis showed that this mating system seems largely male-driven, and that the sexual selection gradients are consistently positive for the male function but change over time to benefit the opposite sex (Anthes et al., 2010; Hoffer et al., 2017; Janicke et al., 2016; Pélissié et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published experimental research on sexual selection.

claim: Due to its pre-eminence as a model system in neuroscience, early molecular studies on L. stagnalis tended to focus on the central nervous system.
source: Due to its pre-eminence as a model system in neuroscience, early molecular studies tended to focus on the central nervous system (Feng et al., 2009; Johnson and Davison, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published molecular studies and inference about research focus.

claim: The favourable anatomical features of L. stagnalis enabled the accumulation of peptidomic data from the mass spectrometry of single neurons.
source: The favourable anatomical features enabled the accumulation of peptidomic data from the mass spectrometry of single neurons (Perry et al., 1999; Worster et al., 1998), making the neuropeptidergic system the most intensely studied part of the central nervous system (Buckett et al., 1990; Perry et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published peptidomic research.

claim: The neuropeptidergic system is the most intensely studied part of the L. stagnalis central nervous system.
source: The favourable anatomical features enabled the accumulation of peptidomic data from the mass spectrometry of single neurons (Perry et al., 1999; Worster et al., 1998), making the neuropeptidergic system the most intensely studied part of the central nervous system (Buckett et al., 1990; Perry et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research and inference about research intensity.

claim: Many sequencing methodologies including Sanger, Illumina, BGISEQ and Oxford Nanopore have been successfully applied to L. stagnalis.
source: Taking advantage of a variety of platforms available for nucleotide sequencing: Sanger (Davison and Blaxter, 2005; Sadamoto et al., 2004; Swart et al., 2019), Illumina (Korneev et al., 2018; Sadamoto et al., 2012; Stewart et al., 2016), BGISEQ (Jehn et al., 2018) and Oxford Nanopore (Fodor et al., 2020a), many sequencing methodologies have been successfully applied to this species.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research using various sequencing platforms.

claim: Extensive genomic, transcriptomic and peptidomic data for L. stagnalis are available in the NCBI database.
source: Extensive genomic, transcriptomic and peptidomic data for L. stagnalis are available in the NCBI database.
evidence: The claim is supported by knowledge of publicly available data resources.
